title: Non-Recognition of Online Doctoral Programs in India in the Era of AI, Education 4.0, and Education 5.0: Challenges for Working Professionals
content: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and digitally mediated learning has intensified debate about flexibility, access, and quality assurance in higher education. This study examines stakeholder perceptions of the non-recognition of fully online doctoral education in India, focusing on career barriers, psychological burnout, acceptance of Education 4.0, institutional resistance, and support for policy reform. Using a cross-sectional questionnaire dataset of 832 respondents, the study applies descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), group comparisons, and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. The findings indicate comparatively high mean scores for perceived career barriers and Education 4.0 acceptance. Group comparisons did not identify statistically significant differences across the categories examined. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F(7, 824) = 64.28, p < 0.001; R² = 0.353; adjusted R² = 0.348). Institutional resistance was positively associated with policy-reform support, whereas career barriers showed a smaller negative association. Education 4.0 acceptance also showed a positive association with reform support. These findings represent statistical relationships within the sample and do not establish causal effects. The study contributes to discussions on Indian higher-education policy by outlining considerations for a quality-assured framework that addresses research supervision, assessment, academic integrity, institutional accountability, and equitable access to doctoral education.
